A Study of Solar Wind Activity and Associated Space Weather Condition

Abstract:

The solar wind is a continuous, supersonic outflow from the solar corona. It permeates the interplanetary space and serves as the primary medium through which various solar activities interact with geospace via a complex series of events commonly called space weather. Studies of solar wind proton number density measurements in near-Earth space show discrete fluctuations at a particular set of frequencies (0.1 - 5 mHz), corresponding to length scales of 100-10,000 Mm), which are prevalent in slow solar Wind (&lt 450 km/s). These are known as periodic density structures (PDSs). Studies on PDSs are limited, yet they provide strong evidence for their solar origin. We have investigated the origin of the PDSs in the slow solar wind by studying them using near-Earth (Wind) and near-Sun (Parker Solar Probe (PSP)) measurements, which show a set of common periodicties. Further, we have investigated the coronal origin of these PDSs using data from the Heliospheric Imager (HI) on board the STEREO-A spacecraft, which reveals the same set of common periodicities as observed earlier in Wind and PSP measurements, providing clear evidence of their coronal nature. Also, we found that these PDSs originate in the solar corona via magnetic reconnection. Sometimes, the density and speed of the solar wind are significantly reduced, known as a ``solar wind disappearance (DSW)&quot event. We have investigated a DSW event observed on both Earth and Mars in December 2022. We have traced the source region of the DSW event to an active region-coronal hole (AR-CH) complex, revealing that a plasma jet eruption reduces the CH area, which eventually leads to the CH's disappearance and the DSW condition. In addition, we have studied the responses of solar wind parameters and energetic particles (ions/electrons) to the forward Interplanetary Shock induced by the passage of Interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs) &nbspand Co-rotating Interaction Regions (CIRs). Our study shows that ICME-driven shocks are more intense than the shocks driven by CIR. As a result, stronger enhancements are observed in the solar wind at the ICME shock front than at the CIR shock front, leading to stronger geomagnetic disturbances.
